<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-structured cases, but A's mechanism survived the exchange better. A's opening laid out a clean deterrence story explicitly bounded by "repeatedly" to exempt honest mistakes, and its Rebuttal 1 pressed a real tension in CON's case (fines are simultaneously "trivial" for big platforms and "devastating" for small agencies). CON's answer that this is "targeting, not incoherence" was adequate but not decisive. The pivotal exchange came when A pointed out that CON's proposed alternative—withholding payment from vendors—is itself a financial penalty for non-compliance, just privately administered by the very agencies CON says are too passive and under-resourced to act. CON never closed this loop: it kept asserting that grants and approved-vendor lists would impose the condition upstream, but never explained what forces agencies or funders to write and enforce those conditions, especially given CON's own claim that these actors are incapable of self-discipline. That left CON's alternative looking like "the same mechanism with the teeth removed," which is exactly A's closing line. CON's targeting critique (fines hit the operator, not the vendor who can actually fix code) remained a genuine and under-answered structural point for A, but A's contract-renegotiation response, plus the internal contradiction A exposed in CON's own remedy, gave A the cleaner, more resolved path to the vote.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's move in Rebuttal 2 (A4.3-A4.5) showing that CON's "withholding payment" alternative is itself an unenforced, self-administered financial penalty was the most damaging and least fully answered exchange; CON's response in Rebuttal 2/closing asserted upstream conditions without ever specifying what compels agencies to adopt or enforce them.</best_rebuttal>
